title: Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves
text:
In the late 1930s, a young psychiatrist named John Bowlby worked at the London Child Guidance Clinic. Among the children referred to him were many who had been caught stealing. He studied 44 of them in detail, interviewing the children and their parents and building up a picture of each family's history, and compared them with a group of children at the clinic who had problems but did not steal.

One group among the thieves stood out. Bowlby described them as "affectionless": they seemed unable to form warm bonds and showed little guilt or feeling for others. When he looked at their histories, most of these children had gone through long separations from their mothers or main caregivers in their early years, because of illness, hospital stays or being moved between homes. Such separations were much rarer in the comparison group.

Bowlby published the study in 1944. It was a small clinical sample without a modern control design, and he later acknowledged its limits. But it set him on the path that led to attachment theory, his reports for the World Health Organization, and changes in how hospitals treated young children, such as allowing parents to visit and stay.
lesson: Early separations and broken bonds can leave marks that show up years later as behavior. When a child acts out, it is worth asking what happened to their connections.
location: London Child Guidance Clinic, London, UK
source: Bowlby, J. (1944). Forty-four juvenile thieves: Their characters and home-life. International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 25, 19-53 and 107-128.
caveat: The study relied on a small clinical sample and retrospective reports, so it showed an association rather than proving that separation caused the behavior.
